content: In individuals diagnosed with cystic fibrosis, there are currently no established guidelines or targets for participation in physical activity. Furthermore, no optimal strategies have been identified to effectively promote engagement in physical activity within this population. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of interventions aimed at increasing participation in physical activity among people with cystic fibrosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register with the terms physiotherapy and exercise. The most recent search was performed on December 5, 2013. Additional searches were carried out in electronic databases such as MEDLINE, CINAHL (Ebscohost), PsycINFO (OvidSP), and the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro). Furthermore, clinical trial registries were reviewed for completed but unpublished studies, with the most recent search conducted on September 10, 2012. The review included all randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that investigated strategies designed to promote increased participation in daily physical activity among individuals with cystic fibrosis. Two independent authors selected studies for inclusion, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus, or by involving a third author for arbitration. Four studies, involving a total of 199 participants, met the inclusion criteria. These studies primarily focused on children with cystic fibrosis, with only one study including both adult and pediatric participants. The methodological descriptions in these studies were insufficient to adequately assess the risk of bias, particularly in terms of blinding of assessors and selective reporting. One study was conducted in an inpatient setting with follow-up in an outpatient setting, while the other three studies were conducted in individuals with stable respiratory disease in outpatient settings. All included studies utilized exercise training as a means to promote participation in physical activity. The duration of the intervention periods varied, ranging from 18 days to three years. However, no improvements in physical activity participation were observed with intervention periods lasting six months or less. Notably, improvements in physical activity participation were only reported in studies where follow-up extended beyond 12 months. None of the intervention strategies demonstrated a significant impact on the quality of life of participants. The authors concluded that, while physical activity is generally considered beneficial for individuals with cystic fibrosis, there is a lack of robust evidence regarding effective strategies to promote the initiation and sustained participation in physical activity within this population. The review provided limited evidence suggesting that activity counseling and exercise advice, delivered over a period of at least six months, may lead to improved physical activity participation when incorporated into a home exercise program. However, further research is necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of alternative strategies, such as health coaching or telemedicine applications, in promoting the uptake and adherence to regular physical activity. Additionally, determining the optimal duration of interventions, including exercise training programs, will be critical in addressing barriers to physical activity participation for individuals with cystic fibrosis.
